title: Briefing a Case
short: A student case brief records the facts, the procedural history, the issue (question presented), the holding, the reasoning and the disposition, and often notes concurrences and dissents.
trouble: Students copy long passages and miss the issue. Write the issue as a yes-or-no question that the holding answers.

blocks.html: Law students prepare for class by writing a case brief: a one-page summary of an opinion in a fixed form. (It is not the same as the long "brief" a lawyer files with a court.) Once you know the parts of an opinion, briefing is a way of pulling out the parts that matter.
A student case brief records the facts, the procedural history, the issue (the question presented), the holding, the reasoning and the disposition, and often notes concurrences and dissents.

head: Heading
What to write
rows: only the facts the court relied on, in a few sentences
what the lower courts did and how the case got here
the legal question, as a yes-or-no question tied to the facts
the answer to the issue, as a rule ("Yes; a plaintiff who…")
why the court decided as it did: the rule's source and how it applied
the main point of any concurrence or dissent

blocks.html: Briefing forces you to decide what the case stands for. Copying passages is easy; stating the issue in one question and the holding in one sentence takes understanding. A good test: the holding should answer the issue exactly, and the reasoning should explain why the answer is yes or no. Your brief is also a tool for telling holding from dicta: anything that does not help answer the issue belongs elsewhere.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: A federal regulation limited a consultation duty under the Endangered Species Act to agency actions in the United States or on the high seas. Wildlife groups sued. Two members said they had visited project areas abroad (in Egypt and Sri Lanka) to see endangered species and hoped to return someday.
opts.reasoning: Article III requires an injury in fact that is concrete and imminent. "Someday" plans to return, with no concrete plans, are not imminent injury. The Court also rejected standing based only on a procedural violation that caused the plaintiffs no concrete harm.
opts.later: Its three-part test for standing is quoted in nearly every standing case.

blocks.cap: A brief of Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992). Reveal each part in turn.

blocks.title: Write the issue
blocks.q: Turn this vague issue into a good one: "Standing."
steps: Tie it to the key facts: members who visited habitats abroad and hoped to return someday.
Name the legal standard: injury in fact under Article III.
blocks.a: Do members of a group who once visited endangered species' habitats abroad and intend to return "someday" suffer an injury in fact that gives them standing under Article III?

blocks.title: Match the holding
blocks.q: Write the holding for that issue.
steps: Keep the key facts and the rule.
blocks.a: No. Vague "someday" intentions to return, without concrete plans, do not show an actual or imminent injury, so the plaintiffs lacked standing.

blocks.html: Copying long passages and missing the issue. Write the issue as a yes-or-no question that the holding answers. Check your brief: if the holding does not begin with "yes" or "no" (or a clear rule) that answers your issue, one of them is wrong.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put the headings of a case brief in the usual order.
